title: Bubble Sort
summary: Sort a short list by swapping neighbours. Trace each bubble sort pass, understand the early stop, and compare programs in six languages.
introduction: Picture children lining up from shortest to tallest. Two neighbours swap places when they are in the wrong order. Bubble sort repeats this idea for numbers. After a trip along the list, one large number has reached its final place.
learningObjectives: Explain when the early-stop rule saves work

blocks.text: A swap exchanges two items. A pass is one trip across the part of the list we are checking. Bubble sort compares neighbours and swaps them when the left value is bigger.
After each pass, the largest value in that area is at the right end. The next pass can stop one position earlier. The swapped flag remembers whether anything moved.

items: Start with [4, 2, 3, 1]. Compare 4 and 2, then swap: [2, 4, 3, 1].
Compare 4 and 3, then 4 and 1. The first pass ends with [2, 3, 1, 4]. The 4 is finished.
On the next pass, 2 and 3 stay put. Swap 3 and 1, giving [2, 1, 3, 4].
On the last pass, swap 2 and 1. The result is [1, 2, 3, 4].

blocks.text: The same program in six languages

Choose the language you are learning. Each tab solves the same problem and prints the same result. JavaScript can run in this page. The other tabs need separate local tools: a C11 compiler, a C++17 compiler, Python 3, .NET 8 or later for C#, or Java 17. Use Program.cs for C# and Main.java for Java.
The four original numbers appear in ascending order. The program prints only the final list; the numbered walk-through shows the work between the start and that output.
Empty and one-item lists need no pass. Negative numbers work with the same comparison. Equal numbers are not swapped because the rule uses >, not >=.

This version changes the input list. It is stable: equal items keep their old relative order because equal neighbours never cross. This matters when numbers are attached to records such as score cards.
How much work and extra room?
For n items, the longest run makes (n - 1) + (n - 2) + ... + 1 comparisons. That grows like n squared, written O(n²). Doubling a large list can make about four times as much work.

If the list is already sorted, one pass makes no swaps and we stop. That gives O(n) best time for this version. Only a few positions, one temporary value, and a flag are stored, so extra space is O(1).

blocks.title: Try one small change
blocks.text: Change the input to [1, 2, 3, 4]. Trace the first pass. swapped stays false, so the next pass is skipped and the output stays the same.

blocks.title: A common mistake
blocks.text: Reset swapped at the start of every pass. If you leave an old true value there, the early stop cannot spot a later pass with no changes. Keep i < end so i + 1 stays inside the list.
